items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Mathematical Prestige: Epistemic Burden, Professional Identity, and Status Threat Under Automated Discovery
items.abstract: Automated mathematical discovery can increase the supply of results while changing the distribution of verification labour, research autonomy, and academic recognition. This theoretical working paper separates epistemic burden, professional identity, status threat, and governance concerns rather than treating opposition as evidence of jealousy. A small additive model distinguishes discovery-label-invariant formal validity from workload and utility. Eight Lean-checked propositions establish conditional workload relations, the possibility of overload, and the non-identification of latent motives from aggregate opposition. Public primary sources provide context but no representative psychological evidence. Deterministic synthetic examples illustrate the assumptions, and a prospective factorial study is proposed to test responses to source labels, verification packages, and credit rules. No participants were recruited and no empirical effects were estimated. The framework’s central contribution is an auditable separation of deductive consequences, documented positions, and hypotheses requiring evidence.

items.title: The impact of GenAI on the future of requirements engineering
items.abstract: Abstract Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), are transforming how we design and build systems by increasing access to domain knowledge and by providing automation support to software engineering (SE). As implementation becomes less expensive through generalist SE agents, engineering effort shifts away from writing correct code and toward expressing, curating, verifying, and evaluating requirements. In this paper, we survey the state of the art in AI for requirements engineering (RE) research leading up to the transformation, before reviewing advances in LLMs. We survey two subsequent research areas: prompt programming, which treats LLM instructions as a program in SE vernacular, and generalist SE agents, which combine multiple LLM advances to yield semi-autonomous processes that complete SE tasks. Finally, we explore the future of requirements engineering along two axes: matters changing how we interact with requirements through the SE process, and matters changing how requirements are experienced by software developers and stakeholders more broadly, including end-users. This article aims to inform how RE researchers can navigate this transformation in the selection of future research priorities.

items.title: The Impact of Imperfect XAI on Human-AI Decision-Making
items.abstract: Explainability techniques are rapidly being developed to improve human-AI decision-making across various cooperative work settings. Consequently, previous research has evaluated how decision-makers collaborate with imperfect AI by investigating appropriate reliance and task performance with the aim of designing more human-centered computer-supported collaborative tools. Several human-centered explainable AI (XAI) techniques have been proposed in hopes of improving decision-makers' collaboration with AI; however, these techniques are grounded in findings from previous studies that primarily focus on the impact of incorrect AI advice. Few studies acknowledge the possibility for the explanations to be incorrect even if the AI advice is correct. Thus, it is crucial to understand how imperfect XAI affects human-AI decision-making. In this work, we contribute a robust, mixed-methods user study with 136 participants to evaluate how incorrect explanations influence humans' decision-making behavior in a bird species identification task taking into account their level of expertise and an explanation's level of assertiveness. Our findings reveal the influence of imperfect XAI and humans' level of expertise on their reliance on AI and human-AI team performance. We also discuss how explanations can deceive decision-makers during human-AI collaboration. Hence, we shed light on the impacts of imperfect XAI in the field of computer-supported cooperative work and provide guidelines for designers of human-AI collaboration systems.

items.title: THE İNFLUENCE OF THE HUMAN FACTOR ON THE EFFECTİVENESS OF ORGANİZATİONAL CHANGE MANAGEMENT AND THE SUCCESS OF TRANSFORMATİON PROJECTS
items.abstract: Modern organizational transformation is characterized by a high degree of technological, organizational, and managerial complexity. Despite significant advances in project and organizational change management methodologies, a significant portion of transformation initiatives fail to deliver the expected results. One reason is the insufficient attention to the human factor, including leadership, employee engagement, readiness for change, communication quality, organizational culture, staff competence, and resistance to change.The purpose of this study is to systematize scientific understanding of the role of the human factor in organizational change management and to develop a conceptual model of its influence on the success of transformation projects. The scientific novelty lies in new approaches—based on an analysis of classical and contemporary research—to consider the human factor not as an auxiliary element, but as an independent determinant of transformation results. The hypothesis is substantiated that the human factor has a direct positive impact on the effectiveness of organizational change management, and the effectiveness of change Management, in turn, positively influences the success of transformation projects. A hypothesis is also proposed regarding the direct influence of the human factor on project success and the effectiveness of change management. The formulated model allows for the integration of research on human behavior, leadership, organizational readiness for change, and project success into a single research construct. The article proposes a methodology for subsequent empirical testing of the model using a questionnaire survey and structural modeling.

items.title: The interpreter as developer: An autoethnographic design study of building a computer-assisted interpreting tool through human-LLM co-creation
items.abstract: Real-time AI captioning now serves audiences at multilingual events, yet computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tools are still built for interpreters, rarely by them. This article reports an autoethnographic design study in which a professional interpreter with no programming training built a local-first CAI system through expert-led 'vibe coding', co-creating with an LLM architect and a coding agent. Analysis of the complete development dialogues shows how tacit professional knowledge, from segmentation to booth infrastructure, was externalized into design after generic defaults failed in use. In a demanding public scientific event, three mechanisms of in-booth appropriation emerge under a firmly human-led division of labor; telemetry from a first fully instrumented assignment shows a fully local chain sustaining a median translation latency of 0.94 s across 971 utterances. The case is read as lead-user innovation newly enabled by generative AI, with implications for the technological literacy of interpreters and the future of interpreter training.

items.title: The moderating role of tough love on relations between servant leadership and follower outcomes
items.abstract: Is servant leadership really a Disneyland-inspired fantasy of sunshine, lollipops, and hand-holding that makes followers complacent and lowers the bottom line of organizations, as critics claim? This criticism overlooks that servant leaders, striving to bring out the full potential in followers, do not only give positive strokes but may also provide followers with critical feedback. To assess the role of critical feedback in mitigating the flaws of servant leadership raised by critics, this study introduces tough love, the delivery of criticism with a positive tone and clear intent to help recipients overcome their deficiencies. We hypothesize that the relationship between servant leadership and key outcomes, such as follower performance, is strengthened the more servant leaders provide followers with tough love. We contend that tough love is appreciated by followers, solidifies relationships with their leaders, and helps them to grow through self-expansion. We reason that this growth benefits their work behaviors and attitudes. With multi-source field data covering three points in time, controlling for positive and negative feedback and prior levels of dependent variables, tough love is shown to moderate relations between servant leadership and both in-role performance and organizational citizenship behaviors, with mixed results for creativity and turnover intentions.

items.title: The Power of Storytelling in Film: Examining AI's Influence on Artistic Expression and Creative Processes
items.abstract: This paper explores the enduring power of storytelling in film and critically examines the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on creative processes within the film industry. Utilizing the Creative Cognition Framework and the Csikszentmihalyi’s Systems Model of Creativity, this study investigates how AI tools influence both generative and exploratory cognitive processes in film storytelling. A qualitative methodology, combining a comprehensive literature review with thematic analysis of questionnaire responses from 20 film and multimedia students at the University of Abuja, Nigeria, reveals nuanced insights. Findings indicate that AI significantly augments creative processes by enhancing efficiency, facilitating idea generation, and streamlining production tasks. However, respondents consistently emphasize AI's limitations in replicating human emotional depth, cultural understanding, and originality, advocating for a hybrid human-AI collaborative approach. The paper contributes to the understanding of human-AI collaboration in creative domains, highlighting opportunities for innovation while reaffirming the irreplaceable essence of human artistry in storytelling.

items.title: The Reasons Research and AI Thrive Together
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research by expanding investigators’ capacity to examine complex information, identify unrecognized relationships, generate hypotheses, and develop innovative solutions to scientific challenges. This article examines the relationship between human scientific expertise and artificial intelligence, emphasizing AI’s computational capabilities alongside the importance of human judgment, methodological rigor, and scientific accountability. Drawing upon peer-reviewed research involving molecular biology, materials science, pharmaceutical discovery, autonomous experimentation, and human–AI collaboration, the investigation demonstrates how computational intelligence can extend scientific inquiry beyond the limitations of conventional research methods. Attention is given to AI-assisted knowledge synthesis, interdisciplinary discovery, hypothesis generation, and the identification of solutions within multidimensional research environments. The article evaluates concerns regarding algorithmic bias, hallucinated information, intellectual originality, research integrity, and the reliability of computationally generated conclusions. It argues that the legitimacy of AI-assisted research should be determined by evidentiary accuracy, methodological transparency, reproducibility, and independent verification rather than the technological origins of research assistance. Ultimately, the article concludes that artificial intelligence does not diminish the intellectual authority or responsibility of human researchers but can amplify their investigative capabilities. The integration of human expertise and computational intelligence represents an emerging scientific paradigm capable of accelerating discovery, broadening research participation, and expanding the boundaries of human knowledge.

items.title: The unbearable (and unsustainable) social impact of AI-generated “cultural monism” and the EU digital legislation
items.abstract: The increasing use of generative AI (genAI) across cultural and (re)creative sectors is indisputable in contemporary times. Within the EU, these systems are classified as “general-purpose AI” models (Recital 99 of the Artificial Intelligence Act – AI Act) and are expected to deliver a wide range of economic and societal benefits, as affirmed in Recital 105 of the Act. Yet, significant concerns have emerged regarding their potential impact on individuals, civil society, and democracy. In the cultural domain, genAI technologies are widely employed to generate outputs often perceived as original. However, scholarly debate has increasingly highlighted the risk that their widespread diffusion may lead to a form of cultural impoverishment – understood as the depletion of cultural pluralism and diversity of artistic expression resulting from the pervasive use of these systems and their underlying architectures, as well as, ultimately, an increasing standardization of the outputs of the algorithmic creative process. These systematic risks are not merely social or political but also carry significant legal implications. The potential effects of genAI on freedom of (artistic) expression and cultural pluralism may, in fact, infringe upon fundamental rights enshrined in international human rights charters. Yet, the role of legal scholarship in addressing such risks remains uncertain. A promising conceptual instrument for tackling this issue is the notion of systemic risk, recently introduced in two key pieces of EU digital legislation: the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the mentioned AI Act. This article examines the advantages and limitations of employing this concept to address the risk of cultural impoverishment. The analysis focuses primarily on the EU legal framework, with particular attention to the AI Act, while adopting a functional and comparative perspective, given that the principal challenges stem from US-based AI systems. It also situates the inquiry within the broader dynamics of the data economy, specifically the logic of knowledge capitalism. The article begins by exploring the potential impacts of genAI on cultural pluralism and artistic expression, assessing whether these may with time culminate in cultural impoverishment – or even a transition toward cultural monism, marked by the predominance, in all the cultural productions, of a single mainstream culture. It then analyses whether EU digital regulation is equipped to subsume such phenomena within the legal category of systemic risk.

items.title: The Unnoticed Freezes in the AI Era
items.abstract: In 2023, 18% of American adults said they had ever used ChatGPT. By early 2026, that number was 44%. AI adoption in the workplace has been even more remarkable. According to Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index, 75% of knowledge workers were already using AI at work, with nearly half having started within the preceding six months. We did not vote to hand over drafting, summarizing, fact-checking, and even thinking to these systems. There was no big decision. Just a free chatbot, a looming deadline, and a prompt that saved twenty minutes. Then another, and another... Regarding this serious issue, I was drawn to a new paper quietly posted on SSRN last September by Professor Vuong Quan Hoang. It gives this slow handover a name: the Correction Freeze Problem (CFP). His question is simple: can a system think it is fine while it is drifting away from reality, and stay that way not because it is lazy or lying, but because the very way it corrects itself makes staying blind the rational choice? The paper answers yes. In four different ways. And when any of those ways meets a world that rewards going along, the drift becomes a trap that is much harder to escape than it was to fall into. To grasp these insights, you don't need the math. Simply because you've lived it.

items.abstract: Risk management is one of the fundamental components of a company's success, whatever its sector of activity. This paper reviews the work done in the field of risk management, both traditionally and by integrating Artificial Intelligence. It highlights the way in which risk management was solved in the traditional way, discussing methods and approaches and citing the limitations of traditional risk management. It also outlines research into the integration of Artificial Intelligence into risk management in the various phases of the risk management process. Based on the open literature published in the various journals in the field of risk management, the stages of the risk management process are the result of human judgment, which may identify risks or, for psychological or/and social reasons, may not, so human subjectivity influences the risk identification phase and all phases of the risk management process. To reduce this subjectivity and to reduce human contact in this phase, our article proposes a model based on Artificial Intelligence that attempts to identify risks and treat them in order to reduce or eliminate existing risks.

items.title: Translators’ Gains and Pains in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: This study aimed to provide a comprehensive systematic review of research published in peer-reviewed scientific journals in Arabic and English between 2022 and 2026 that investigated the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Copilot, and others, on translation and translation education among professional translators, translation students, and faculty members. The study used the PRISMA 2020 framework for systematic search, screening, and documentation, and employed a thematic analysis approach based on the model developed by Braun and Clarke. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria to 24 initial records, the final analysis included 18 studies. The findings revealed that the most significant benefits of using generative AI tools included improved efficiency and productivity, reduced time to complete translation tasks, support for post-editing processes, improved certain translation quality indicators, and the promotion of self-directed learning and the development of professional competencies among translators and students. At the same time, the results identified several challenges, most notably terminological accuracy issues, difficulties handling cultural and idiomatic expressions and local dialects, risks associated with overreliance on intelligent systems, and ethical concerns involving privacy, transparency, and professional accountability. The review also showed that the impact of generative AI varies by text type, specialized domain, and the assessment tools used. In addition, it highlighted limited evidence available concerning the Arabic language, particularly in areas such as legal translation, idiomatic expressions, and local dialects. This study contributes an interpretive framework based on the concept of “Gains and Pains” to explain generative AI’s dual impact on translation and translation education. The findings conclude that generative AI does not fully replace human translators; rather, it serves as a supportive tool that reshapes translators’ professional roles toward reviewing, verifying, and evaluating outputs. Accordingly, the study recommends integrating generative AI tools into translator training programs within clear pedagogical and ethical frameworks. They should also include post-editing, critical thinking, and output-verification skills, and support further specialized applied research in the Arab context.

items.title: Transparent Information Flow Modeling for Role-Aware AI Act Assessment
items.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a structured framework for governing high-risk AI systems, emphasizing transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability. However, current assessment practices often rely on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists, limiting their ability to capture the socio-technical complexity of real-world deployments. We explore the use of the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), a modeling-based approach to AI Act compliance assessment. IFM represents decision systems -- whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid -- as networks of information sites and transformation channels, enabling structured analysis of how information, decisions, and responsibilities flow across organizational and technical boundaries. We apply IFM in a real-world case involving a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, evaluating both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. Our results demonstrate that IFM can serve as a scaffold to bridge both component-based and holistic perspectives, and how technical systems are situated within socio-technical contexts. In doing so, IFM supports transparency, identifies risk pathways, and enables alignment analysis between intended and actual use. We argue that such modeling provides a foundational tool for effective, context-sensitive AI governance and accountability -- offering capabilities beyond conventional checklist-based assessments.

items.title: TrustGuard: A Risk-Aware Human Oversight Framework for Safe Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents can perform increasingly consequential actions on behalf of users, creating a need for human oversight that is proportional to the potential risk of each action. This paper presents TrustGuard, a lightweight and interpretable risk-aware human oversight framework for AI agents. TrustGuard automatically evaluates proposed actions using five factors: privacy risk, financial risk, data modification risk, irreversibility risk, and external impact. Each factor is scored from zero to five, producing a total score from zero to twenty-five. Based on the score, actions are classified as Low, Medium, or High Risk and mapped to autonomous execution, user confirmation, or human approval. A prototype was implemented using Python and Streamlit to demonstrate the framework. The rule-based analyzer was calibrated using 120 development scenarios and subsequently evaluated on a held-out pilot set of 30 new scenarios. TrustGuard correctly classified 27 of the 30 test scenarios, achieving 90 percent accuracy. The results demonstrate the potential of transparent risk-based oversight while also identifying limitations in detecting some security-sensitive and privacy-sensitive actions.

items.title: USE OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR DESIGNING ROBOTIC MODELS USING ENGINEERING GRAPHICS
items.abstract: The article examines the possibilities of using generative artificial intelligence in teaching the discipline “Engineering and Computer Graphics” in the design of robotic models for the processing industry. The feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence models into the design process of robotic systems as a means of developing spatial thinking, graphic competence, design skills, and digital skills of agricultural university students is substantiated. It is established that modern generative systems (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Claude, DALL·E, etc.) support all stages of educational design, from developing technical specifications and generating product concepts to creating drawings and three-dimensional models, visualizing designs, preparing technical documentation, and analyzing possible design solutions. A methodology for using generative artificial intelligence in the educational project “Design of a Robotic Manipulator” is proposed. The methodology is based on the principles of project-based learning, STEM education, the competency-based approach, and the use of CAD systems. A structural model for integrating generative artificial intelligence into the process of graphic training has been developed. It includes the stages of problem formulation, concept generation, sketch creation, three-dimensional modeling, preparation of design documentation, and expert evaluation of the finished product. It is demonstrated that the use of generative AI contributes to increasing students’ motivation, developing engineering thinking, fostering digital literacy, and reducing the time required for routine operations in the design of robotic models.

items.title: What AI pretends to be?
items.abstract: Abstract Recent research shows that anthropomorphizing of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, such as virtual assistants or chatbots, affects users’ trust. This paper explores what an AI technology should look like at the interface to facilitate appropriate trust. It proposes an integrated framework based on related work, including Lee and See’s (2004) trust in automation model, Mollerup’s (2019) pretense design, as well as Clark and Fischer’s (2023) notion of depictions, for analysis and design of appearances of AI applications that pretend to be something different. Following the proposed framework, cases of AI applications are analyzed. They span a spectrum of appearances, from humans with open or specifc identities, through talking animals, to plants. Analyses suggest that appearances of AI applications should faithfully reflect the actual ability, characteristics, and design intent, in order to facilitate users’ trustworthiness assessments of the applications. Lastly, design implications and future research are discussed.

items.title: What is user engagement? revisited: A comprehensive review of the concept of user engagement from 2010 to 2025. An Annual Review of Information Science and Technology (ARIST) paper
items.abstract: Abstract User engagement (UE) has long been proposed as a holistic framework for understanding user‐technology interactions and a mediator for outcomes of digital technology use, such as learning, health behavior change, information acquisition, and social connectivity. This literature review, encompassing 367 multidisciplinary, empirical journal and conference papers, investigated how UE was conceptualized between 2010 and 2025 by examining authors' implicit and explicit definitions of UE, use of theoretical frameworks, and methods for operationalizing the concept. Among the key findings, UE was consistently conceptualized as behavior, affect, cognition, social interaction, and future intention. Yet, behavioral approaches were dominant; limited attention was placed on cognitive engagement. In addition, the use of theoretical frameworks and explicit definitions in the studies was lacking, and UE was frequently treated as the outcome variable in the research, rather than as a mediator for other outcomes. The implications of these results are discussed with respect to a digital UE research agenda. Ultimately, I argue that the concept of UE has devolved through increased emphasis on behavioral engagement, and that we must rethink behavioral, cognitive, and affective engagement to be more aligned with user goals and agency.

items.title: When AI Is—and Is Not—Needed: AI Literacy and Computational Thinking in Primary STEM
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly present in children’s lives, yet exposure does not necessarily lead to an accurate understanding of how AI works. This study examined whether a LEGO-based integrated STEM intervention could improve third-grade students’ AI literacy and computational thinking, particularly their ability to distinguish machine learning from rule-based automation and reason about training data, model error, and technology choice. An embedded mixed-methods, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control-group design was conducted with 93 students from four intact classrooms. The experimental group (n = 46) completed eight weeks of authentic design problems, while the control group (n = 47) continued regular Life Studies instruction. After controlling for pretest scores, the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in AI literacy, F(1, 90) = 152.51, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.629, and computational thinking, F(1, 90) = 22.18, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.198. Qualitative evidence showed a shift from viewing AI through robots and automatic actions toward reasoning about learning from examples, data diversity, limitations, human oversight, accessibility, and problem–technology fit. Integrated STEM instruction can foster critical AI literacy by making AI mechanisms visible and inviting students to judge whether AI is needed at all.

items.title: When Execution Is Cheap: Specification, Evaluation, and Rent Capture in AI-Enabled Work
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence lowers the cost of executing well-specified tasks, economic value may shift toward defining desired outcomes and evaluating machine-generated outputs. This paper examines the conditions under which that shift creates economic rents and identifies who may capture them. It separates defining success into four activities: eliciting intent, selecting among admissible specifications, ratifying a choice, and validating outputs. Two models clarify the underlying mechanisms. The first shows that gains from cheaper execution approach a ceiling determined by evaluation cost, which makes evaluator attention more consequential as generation becomes inexpensive. The second shows that generating more candidates increases the marginal value of proxy fidelity, linking abundant output to specification overfitting and Goodhart-type failures. These mechanisms indicate where value may concentrate without determining who receives the returns. Rent requires inelastic supply, exclusion from the created surplus, and the absence of cheaper substitutes. These conditions are most likely when specifications scale across many executions, ratification carries liability, trust institutions certify judgment, organizational systems control codified knowledge, or concentrated model providers set influential defaults. The analysis further distinguishes machine-checkable evaluation against a stated specification from a principal’s assessment of fit to purpose. The former is increasingly commoditized; the latter remains tied to authority, attention, and accountability. The paper develops six testable predictions and a factorial experiment examining evaluation costs, specification fidelity, authority drift, and psychological ownership. Cheap execution relocates bottlenecks, while institutions and market structure determine whether specification, evaluation, default setting, or scarce execution inputs generate rents and who captures them.

items.title: When Recognition Should Remain Silent
items.abstract: The Difference Between Being Remembered and Being Understood There is something profoundly human about the experience of being remembered. A familiar voice, a shared reference, or an acknowledgment of something that mattered in an earlier encounter can transform an otherwise ordinary exchange into one characterized by continuity. We recognize that our history has not disappeared simply because the previous conversation ended. In human relationships, this continuity can become a foundation for trust, familiarity, and the gradual development of shared understanding. Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of participating in certain computational dimensions of this process. Persistent memory enables systems to retrieve earlier conversations, recognize recurring preferences, resume unfinished activities, and adapt their responses to the histories of individuals with whom they interact. As these capacities converge with multimodal perception and embodied robotics, artificial agents may also begin to initiate interactions based on what they believe they know about a person. Yet this development introduces a distinction that deserves greater attention: remembering someone accurately is not necessarily the same as understanding how to respond to them appropriately. Consider a companion robot that recognizes an individual returning home after a difficult day. Through previous encounters, the system may have learned that the person sometimes appreciates conversation or reassurance during stressful circumstances. Its memory could be accurate, its recognition successful, and its conversational response entirely consistent with earlier preferences. Nevertheless, initiating a supportive exchange may be precisely the wrong action if the person presently needs solitude, concentration, or the freedom to remain unobserved.

items.title: Who Frames, Who Acts, Who Learns? Allocating Decision Rights for Agentic AI in Graduate Medical Education, Clinical Research, and Clinical Care
items.abstract: Background: Health care organizations are deploying artificial intelligence (AI) agents faster than they are deciding who holds authority over the decisions those agents touch. In June 2026, the MIT Center for Information Systems Research (CISR) published the AI Decision Matrix, which assigns humans and AI to three decision components (frame, act, and learn) along two dimensions: ambiguity and risk. The framework was derived from executives in telecommunications, financial services, manufacturing, and law, and it has not been examined in health care. Methods: We conducted a structured conceptual analysis. We operationalized the two dimensions with health care anchors, assembled an inventory of 18 recurring decisions across graduate medical education (GME), clinical research operations, and clinical care, and classified each decision by quadrant. We then compared the framework’s default human and AI assignments with the accountability requirements of the ACGME, 21 CFR, ICH E6(R3), FDA clinical decision support guidance, the ONC HTI-1 rule, and the EU AI Act. Results: Five decisions were classified as Routine, four as Consequential, four as Exploratory, and five as Strategic. Health care regulation altered the framework’s defaults in two systematic ways. A licensure floor requires a named professional in the act component of 5 of the 18 decisions, including two in which the source framework assigns the act to AI. A learning floor makes outcome ownership a human responsibility in every decision that affects a patient, trainee, or research participant, including Routine ones. We also identified quadrant drift, in which tools introduced as low-risk pilots migrate into high-risk use without reclassification. Conclusions: The AI Decision Matrix offers health care leaders a practical vocabulary for allocating decision rights, but it requires two domain-specific constraints and a reclassification trigger before adoption. We propose an adapted matrix and recommend empirical validation through a modified Delphi study and prospective institutional audits.

items.title: Who is the 'I' in AI? Establishing Decentralized Identity and Accountability for Autonomous Agents
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous AI agents in decentralized ecosystems challenges existing identity paradigms. While human identity is traditionally anchored in biological and/or self-asserted attributes and government credentials, AI agents lack a standardized definition of selfhood, creating critical gaps in trust and accountability. This paper introduces a novel framework for establishing Decentralized AI Identity rooted in Self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles. We propose a formal model that clearly distinguishes human users and AI agents, enabling distinct verification logic for each class while maintaining a unified identity calculus. The central to our contribution is the ABCD Framework, a multi-layered approach to agent identification and verification: (A) Algorithmic Fingerprint, which binds the identity to static model architectures and provenance; (B) Behavioural Fingerprint, which verifies dynamic performance metrics over time; (C) Cryptographic Identity, which anchors the agent via Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and (D) Delegation, which cryptographically binds agent actions to respective human accountability. By orthogonalizing these dimensions, we model how systems can enforce granular trust policies ranging from simple authentication to complex liability assignment, thereby solving the black box identity problem in the autonomous economic activities of AI agents.

items.title: Why disaster experience does not always improve Preparedness: The role of disaster learning and heterogeneous effects
items.abstract: The frequency and severity of natural disasters and public emergencies have continued to increase worldwide. Household preparedness plays a vital role in disaster risk reduction, yet the effect of disaster-related experience on preparedness remains inconclusive. Using survey data from 5,862 residents in China, this study separately examines the associations of past disaster experience and disaster learning with household preparedness. Conventional regression models and a causal forest approach are used to estimate average associations and explore heterogeneous effects across individuals. The results show that disaster learning, rather than past disaster experience, is positively associated with preparedness behavior, highlighting the importance of capacity building. In addition, both past disaster experience and disaster learning exhibit heterogeneous effects across individuals. Feature importance analysis further indicates that social capital, emergency awareness, and community infrastructure are important influential factors associated with preparedness behavior. By introducing a causal forest approach to distinguish the differential effects of past disaster experience and disaster learning, this study provides a more nuanced understanding of household preparedness and offers useful insights for developing more targeted household disaster risk reduction strategies.

items.title: Why Secure AI Adoption Is a Board-Level Priority
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from isolated experimentation into everyday enterprise workflows, knowledge repositories, business applications, and increasingly agentic systems. This paper argues that secure AI adoption should be treated as an enterprise governance and business-risk issue rather than as a narrowly scoped information-technology project. It proposes the Five Pillars of Secure AI Adoption, an author-developed framework comprising governance and accountability, data protection, identity and least privilege, AI-specific security controls, and monitoring and incident response. The framework provides an executive-oriented operating model informed by established resources, including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the NIST Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, and OWASP guidance for large-language-model and generative-AI application security. The paper concludes that security should enable responsible AI innovation through explicit ownership, controlled access, bounded agency, AI-aware safeguards, and observable operations.

items.title: WP-AI-8.4: The Capability-Safety-Responsibility Alignment Framework
items.abstract: WP-AI-8.4 develops a Capability-Safety-Responsibility Alignment Framework for governing the release of advanced AI systems into society. The paper begins from a structural distinction: capability advancement and social release are not the same governance question. Scientific and engineering progress determines what AI can do; governance must separately determine what capabilities may enter society, under what safety conditions, through whose authority, and with what responsibility attached. The framework argues that capability growth does not itself create a right to release. Social release should be justified by necessity, demonstrated governability, appropriate safety conditions, and an identifiable responsibility structure. Release is treated as a graduated and reversible process rather than a one-time product event, and material capability expansion after deployment is defined as a form of capability creep that should trigger renewed review. The paper further proposes that release boundaries should be defined by real-world exposure rather than by labels such as testing, evaluation, or experimentation. Where high-risk systems require realistic testing, the paper introduces the concept of a high-fidelity isolated “Shadow World” in which relevant real-world complexity can be reproduced without exposing the open world to uncontrolled experimental consequences. Drawing on the governance logic used in high-consequence technologies such as nuclear systems, the framework emphasizes staged safety review, staged authorization, cumulative responsibility, and legal accountability across the development, approval, deployment, configuration, and operational chain. It also introduces a non-propagation responsibility: organizations deploying generative AI should be responsible for ensuring that failures within their own controlled environment do not propagate into external networks, other institutions, unrelated users, or society. WP-AI-8.4 builds on the preceding papers in the WP-AI-8 series. WP-AI-8.1 established the engineering circuit-breaker principle; WP-AI-8.2 examined responsibility escape; WP-AI-8.3 connected capability control and human responsibility through a dual-track governance framework. WP-AI-8.4 extends this architecture to the release boundary itself, asking when and under what conditions AI capability may move from controlled development into social deployment.

items.title: “It Works, but I Don’t Know Why”: Uncritical Use, Verification Behavior and Perceived Understanding in Non-CS Students’ Generative AI-Assisted Programming Projects
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) enables students with little programming experience to produce working software, raising the concern that learners may build artifacts they cannot explain. This convergent mixed-methods study examined how uncritical GenAI use and verification behavior (VB) relate to novices’ self-reported understanding of their own AI-assisted projects. Participants were undergraduates from predominantly non-computing majors in two offerings of a general-education Python course; 64 provided complete survey data and 68 written reflections were thematically analyzed. Uncritical use (UR) was associated with a larger self-reported product–understanding gap (GAP; r = 0.43, p < 0.001) but showed little association with perceived understanding (PU), whereas VB was associated with PU (r = 0.45, p < 0.001) but showed little association with the gap. Tests of dependent correlations confirmed that these associations differed. In the reflections, execution-based checking was the most commonly reported verification strategy (47 of 68), whereas comprehension-oriented strategies were less common. Because all measures were self-reported and cross-sectional, the findings are correlational; they suggest that instruction should explicitly scaffold comprehension-oriented verification in AI-integrated introductory programming.

items.title: "Role of Digital Education Innovation in Building a Technologically Literate Society: A Conceptual Study with Reference to Generation Z Students"
items.abstract: In the twenty-first century, digital technology brought about extensive changes in the nature, process, and objectives of education. Moving beyond traditional teacher-centered and classroom-centered teaching, education is now advancing towards online learning, blended learning, smart classrooms, mobile learning, digital teaching resources, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based teaching. In this context, Generation Z students are particularly important because their social and educational environment has developed alongside digital technologies. Technological media has made the teaching-learning process more flexible, participatory, and student-centered. Generation Z is the generation that has grown up with digital technologies. Thus, digital education innovation is not merely a means of modernizing the teaching process; it is also an important means of developing technological literacy among students. The objective of this conceptual research paper is to clarify the conceptual relationship between digital education innovation and technological literacy with reference to Generation Z students. In this study, digital education innovation is viewed as an educational process in which digital devices, online teaching, AI-based technologies, digital resources, and innovative teaching methods are effectively used. Technological literacy refers to students’ ability to understand, use, evaluate, and to employ technological devices and digital resources safely and responsibly. This paper argues that effective digital education innovation can provide a strong foundation for students’ technological competence, digital problem-solving ability, information evaluation ability, and digital citizenship. At the same time, it is necessary to pay attention to challenges such as the digital divide, technological inequality, digital safety, teacher training, availability of technological resources, misinformation, privacy, cybersecurity, and uncontrolled use of artificial intelligence.

items.title: A New Approach to Human Factors Management
items.abstract: This paper proposes a new approach to managing the human factor within an occupational safety management system. The approach is based on viewing the human factor as the interaction between two complex nonlinear dynamic systems: “human characteristics” and “working conditions.” The authors introduce a quantitative assessment of the human factor by comparing the worker’s actual set of abilities–intellectual, sensory, protective, and physical–with the required set of abilities determined by the working conditions. A model of a personal occupational safety management system has been developed. This system forms part of an individual’s self-management system and is responsible for preserving the worker’s life and health. A method for assessing the effectiveness of this system is also proposed, based on the difference between the actual and required abilities to manage personal occupational safety measures. Based on the proposed model, a technology for continuous rapid workplace training has been developed. It is aimed at forming sustainable safe-behavior skills among workers. The paper presents an analysis of the results of implementing this technology at industrial enterprises, which demonstrated a 1.5- to 3-fold reduction in occupational injuries over a period of one to two years. It was established that workers displaying a safe type of behavior experience occupational injuries eight times less frequently than those displaying unsafe behavior. The authors conclude that the proposed approach is highly effective in practice as a tool for the large-scale development of safe behavior.

items.title: A Study on the Factors Associated with College Students’ Intention to Use AI-Based Mental Health Services: The Roles of Trust, Empathy, and Privacy Concern
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence technology is gradually being integrated into mental health service contexts and is increasingly discussed as a potential supplementary resource to university mental health support systems. However, AI-based mental health services involve sensitive factors such as emotional expression, personal privacy, and relational interaction. Therefore, college students’ willingness to accept AI-based mental health services and the potential factors associated with such acceptance remain unclear. Based on an extended Technology Acceptance Model, this study introduces six factors—Accessibility (ACC), Privacy Concern (PC), Perceived Anthropomorphism (PA), Perceived Empathy (EMP), Trust (TRU), and Perceived Usefulness (PU)—to systematically examine their relationships with university students’ Behavioral Intention (BI) to use AI-based mental health services. A total of 375 volunteers participated in the current study and completed relevant questionnaires. Structural equation modeling was employed for data analysis. The results indicate that accessibility, perceived usefulness, and trust are all significantly and positively associated with behavioral intention. Perceived empathy is significantly and positively associated with trust, whereas privacy concern is significantly and negatively associated with both trust and behavioral intention. The analysis of indirect effects shows that there is a significant sequential indirect association between perceived anthropomorphism and behavioral intention through perceived empathy, trust, and perceived usefulness. In addition, a significant negative indirect association between privacy concern and behavioral intention through trust was observed. The findings indicate that, in the highly sensitive context of mental health services, college students’ intention to use AI-based mental health services is associated with a combination of accessibility, perceived usefulness, emotional interaction experience, privacy-related evaluations, and trust.

items.title: Active Learning Strategies on Teacher Education Students’ Attitude and Level of Engagement
items.abstract: This study investigated the dynamics of student engagement within active learning environments, specifically analyzing the relationships between students' attitudes and their behavioral, emotional, and cognitive involvement. Utilizing quantitative research, particularly a descriptive-correlational research design, this study identified the levels of student engagement and evaluated its relationship with their attitude in active learning activities. Through complete enumeration sampling, 44 teacher education students were identified, and their responses were analyzed through weighted means and the Pearson (r) product-moment correlation coefficient. Findings revealed that students are "Highly Engaged" across all measured dimensions, with Grand Means for Behavioral (M=3.78), Emotional (M=3.84), and Cognitive Engagement (M=3.77) reflecting substantial student investment. Statistical analysis confirmed significant positive correlations (p < 0.001) between students' attitudes—notably their Willingness to Participate and Perceived Usefulness—and their engagement levels. Specifically, the strong correlation between Willingness to Participate and Cognitive Engagement (r = 0.79) suggested that students’ internal readiness is closely associated with metacognitive processing and deep learning. The study concluded that engagement may be understood as a dynamic and reciprocal system in which positive attitudes are strongly linked to meaningful learning processes. The practical implications suggest that educators should prioritize confidence-building, low-stakes activities, and structured peer-facilitation roles to help create a supportive classroom community. By fostering a positive “Attitude Filter,” instructors may enhance conditions that support student retention and academic mastery.

items.title: Agent Sociodrama: Social-Dynamics-Guided Persona Recasting for LLM Agent Teams
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned. We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams. Under fixed personas, agents' emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and shape their subsequent interactions. Across six LLM backbones and five social scenarios, we assess social fidelity through classical social-theory patterns and agreement with human judgments. The resulting trajectories exhibit structured social patterns and model-specific differences. We then introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting (TPR), which diagnoses group-dynamic failures from interaction transcripts and social trajectories and recasts agent personas before rerunning the task. Across four collaborative benchmarks, TPR improves performance from both heterogeneous and randomly initialized agent persona compositions, yielding up to 83.3%p of accuracy improvement over the initial casting. On representative distributed-information cooperation and mixed-motive bargaining tasks, we outperform SOTOPIA and AgentVerse in three of four comparisons, by up to 37.5%p in Pareto rate. These results show that validated social trajectories provide actionable signals for repairing LLM agent teams.

items.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.

items.title: ArguScale: Evidence-Grounded Human-AI Sensemaking Across Concurrent Live Conversations
items.abstract: Monitoring concurrent classroom collaborative reasoning discussions is challenging because instructors have to track collaboration-relevant behaviors across multiple ongoing conversations at once. Existing Human-AI conversational sensemaking systems can scale monitoring upward through summaries and visual abstractions, but these representations may distance users from underlying conversational evidence, e.g., relevant audio and transcript segments, needed to forage downward. Through our formative study, we developed ArguScale, an evidence-grounded Human-AI sensemaking system that organizes interactional signals into temporally aligned representations linked to transcript and audio evidence. A temporal signal-density view provides temporal context and supports rapid cross-group comparison, while selective evidence access allows instructors to inspect audio and transcript. We evaluated ArguScale in a mixed-design study with 20 participants. Compared to other conditions, ArguScale improved participants' ability to efficiently and accurately identify collaboration-relevant cues. We further identify strategies participants used to forage for and make sense of conversational evidence under live time constraints.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare in practice: tools, applications and perspectives for clinicians, researchers and educators — an international educational review
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction: The digital transformation of healthcare systems has been accompanied, since the early 2020s, by the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), further accelerated by the emergence of generative AI and large language models (LLMs). Beyond broad discussions about the potential of AI, healthcare professionals, researchers, and educators need practical guidance regarding available tools, their applications, performance, limitations, and the conditions required for their responsible use. Objective: To provide an international, critical, and educational synthesis of the major applications of AI in clinical practice, biomedical research, and health sciences education, while examining its potential benefits, limitations, associated risks, and the conditions required for safe and responsible use, particularly in resource limited settings. Methods: A structured narrative review of the literature was conducted using publications indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. The literature search was supplemented by institutional documents from the World Health Organization (WHO), UNESCO, and the European Union, as well as selected systematic reviews, evidence syntheses, and regional reports addressing the use of AI in healthcare in sub Saharan Africa. Publications primarily published between 2020 and 2026 were prioritized. Results: Available evidence demonstrates a rapid diversification of AI applications in healthcare. Generative AI systems and LLMs can support medical information synthesis and interpretation, clinical decision support, literature searching, scientific writing and communication, development of educational materials, clinical simulation, and selected epidemiological surveillance activities. These technologies may improve access to information and increase the efficiency of selected healthcare and research tasks. However, their use is associated with important risks, including hallucinations and factual errors, algorithmic bias, potential breaches of data privacy, limited traceability and accountability, and the risk of cognitive dependence among users. These challenges are particularly relevant in healthcare systems with limited human, digital, and regulatory resources. Perspectives: Between 2026 and 2030, advances in multimodal AI, agentic systems, and personalized medicine may substantially expand the scope of AI applications in healthcare. These developments will require robust governance frameworks, scientific validation, human oversight, data protection, and appropriate professional training. Particular attention should be given to the linguistic, cultural, technological, and socioeconomic adaptation of AI solutions to resource limited settings to prevent the widening of existing digital and health inequities. Conclusion: The key challenge is no longer whether AI will be used in healthcare, but how it can be implemented safely, ethically, scientifically, and in alignment with the needs of healthcare professionals and populations. In low and middle income countries, particularly in the Sahel, AI integration should be approached as a gradual process based on rigorous validation, human oversight, capacity building, and context specific governance. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; machine learning; generative artificial intelligence; large language models; clinical decision support; ethics; data privacy; medical education; biomedical research; sub Saharan Africa.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN TEACHING NATURAL SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS DISCIPLINES: SURVEY RESULTS ON TEACHERS' AND STUDENTS' READINESS, BARRIERS AND NEEDS
items.abstract: The article presents the results of a survey of 99 teachers of natural science and mathematics disciplines and 195 students in grades 7–11 in Poltava region on the use of AI tools in the educational process. It was found that 96% of teachers and 93.8% of students already use AI, but 64.6% of students did so without any pedagogical guidance. The main systemic barrier for teachers is work overload (66.7%), despite a strong willingness to learn (81.8%). A thematic analysis of students' open-ended responses revealed a dominant message: AI is used primarily to understand material, not to copy it. A critical research gap was identified regarding the specific impact of AI on adolescents as a distinct age group.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Era of Globalisation: Implications for Students' Attitudes, Socialization and Career Perspectives in India
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a significant component of the contemporary globalised world, influencing education, communication, employment, and daily social interactions. Its growing presence in higher education is transforming how students gather information, complete academic tasks, communicate with others, and prepare for their careers. This article analyses the impact of AI on students' attitudes, socialisation, and professional perspectives, particularly within the Indian context. The study employs a qualitative methodology based on secondary data, using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, government policy documents, and reports from recognised national and international institutions. The analysis shows that while students generally acknowledge AI's educational value, factors such as institutional support, perceived benefits, ethical concerns, and trust in AI-generated information shape their attitudes. Although AI can facilitate learning and collaborative educational activities, overreliance on it—at the expense of human interaction—may raise concerns about social engagement and interpersonal relationships. Regarding employment, AI is simultaneously transforming existing professions, creating new job opportunities, and altering the skill sets expected of graduates. According to the World Economic Forum, the transformation of the labour market by 2030 could lead to the creation of 170 million new jobs and the displacement of 90 million, resulting in a net increase of 78 million jobs. India is addressing these changes through initiatives such as the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, India AI FutureSkills, and NITI Aayog’s roadmap for job creation in the AI economy. The article represents the acceptance of a human-oriented model for mixing AI into Indian higher education—one that coordinates technical expertise with critical thinking, academic honesty, social involvement, employability, and moral accountability.

items.title: Assessing User-Subjective Experience with Conversational Agents for Behavioral and Mental Health Interventions: Design and Psychometric Evaluation of CUE-Chat
items.abstract: While AI-conversational agents are increasingly integrated into behavioral and mental health interventions, standardized instruments to assess their performance remain scarce. To address this gap, we developed an instrument to measure user-subjective experience with AI-driven agents in the healthcare domain. We focused on user perception due to its direct contribution to intervention effects, and on healthcare given that the rapid adoption of AI-agents in this domain continues to outpace the development of validated evaluation instruments. Across four studies, we developed and tested the Chatbot User Evaluation instrument (CUE-Chat). First, we identified relevant assessment domains and items through literature review, existing instruments, input from AI-driven agents, and the research team’s domain expertise. Following this, we requested feedback on draft subscales, definitions, and items from expert and laypeople panels. We then tested the structure of the instrument’s concept version. Finally, we conducted a psychometric evaluation and finalized the instrument.CUE-Chat consists of four factors: Perceived Efficacy (4 items), Usability (4 items), Intelligence (4 items), and Safety and Risk Management (4 items). Reliability and validity of the total score and each subscale was good to excellent (Cronbach’s α = .73-.92; Ω = .74-.93). Predictive validity was strong with all scales predictive of users’ overall rating of an AI-agent’s performance.We conclude that CUE-Chat’s strong psychometric properties are promising, and that it is particularly useful for researchers integrating AI-driven agents into behavioral and mental health interventions in both developmental and evaluative stages.

items.title: Authentic assessment in an AI-integrated qualitative research methods course
items.abstract: Abstract Authentic assessment has been a recognized aspiration in higher education for nearly four decades, yet its implementation at the undergraduate level has remained constrained by the procedural demands of professional-level work. Generative artificial intelligence reshapes the implementation calculus by lowering the entry barriers that previously confined authentic assessment to capstone courses, professional programs, and elite institutional contexts. This paper presents a single-semester case study of an AI-integrated qualitative research methods course taught to undergraduates in a child and adolescent development program at a regional public university. Twenty-one students used a custom AI class companion without restriction to produce full-length qualitative research manuscripts. The analytic backbone is a five-dimensional model of authentic assessment, with its physical-context dimension extended to require AI inclusion in fields where professional practice now incorporates the technology. Three rubric-proximal proxy indicators were estimated across the corpus: methods specificity, claim-evidence coupling, and theory-interpretation linkage density. The methods specificity proxy compresses toward the upper bound of its scale, indicating that AI scaffolding supports structural elements of qualitative writing effectively. The two judgment-dependent proxies retain wide dispersion. Process tracing of four contrasting cases identifies three pathways that distinguish stronger from weaker outcomes: criteria-based orchestration, irreducible input supply, and substantive iteration. The boundary-condition pattern indicates that authentic assessment in AI-integrated courses remains diagnostic where it needs to be and is supported where it needed support.

items.abstract: Perkembangan generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) telah mengubah cara mahasiswa memperoleh, mengolah, dan menghasilkan pengetahuan di pendidikan tinggi. Kemudahan memperoleh jawaban secara instan meningkatkan efisiensi pembelajaran, tetapi juga berpotensi mendorong cognitive offloading dan mengurangi keterlibatan mahasiswa dalam proses berpikir. Artikel ini bertujuan menganalisis pembelajaran mendalam (deep learning pedagogy) sebagai respons pedagogis terhadap disrupsi GenAI serta merumuskan reorientasi peran AI dari answer machine menjadi thinking partner. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan desain analisis konseptual melalui sintesis literatur ilmiah, teori, dan dokumen kebijakan mengenai GenAI, cognitive offloading, konstruktivisme, berpikir kritis, metakognisi, dan pembelajaran mendalam. Hasil sintesis menunjukkan bahwa persoalan utama penggunaan GenAI bukan keberadaan cognitive offloading, melainkan pendelegasian aktivitas kognitif yang menggantikan proses berpikir yang menjadi tujuan pembelajaran. Artikel ini merumuskan efficiency–depth paradox, yaitu ketegangan antara peningkatan efisiensi melalui AI dan kebutuhan untuk mempertahankan kedalaman proses belajar. Pembelajaran mendalam melalui prinsip mindful, meaningful, dan joyful learning dapat berfungsi sebagai pedagogical safeguards. Reorientasi AI sebagai thinking partner menempatkan mahasiswa sebagai primary thinker, sementara AI berfungsi sebagai scaffolding untuk questioning, exploration, feedback, verification, dan reflection.

items.title: Decision Theory and Artificial Intelligence: An Anatomical Review of Output Contracts, Acquisition Geometries, and Epistemic Verticals
items.abstract: This paper presents a detailed anatomical review of Miquel Noguer i Alonso's "Decision Theory and Artificial Intelligence" (2026). The reviewed work develops a unified Bayesian decision-theoretic framework that links feasible action spaces, reward functions, statistical estimation targets, and costly information acquisition policies. Central contributions include minimal output contracts for specified reward families (Theorem 4.5), regret propagation decompositions (Proposition 6.1), capacity-constrained optimal gates with complementary slackness (Theorem 7.1), an acquisition-output contract characterising compressed representations that preserve nonnegative-price routing decisions (Theorem 7.6), and a routing-geometry dichotomy between discrete decisions (information most valuable near action boundaries) and continuous quadratic sizing (precision gains favouring strongest signals) (Proposition 7.13). The framework accommodates supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, large language models, and typed probability interfaces such as JEV. A retrospective empirical study of 27,241 LLM cases evaluates cost-aware replacement routing. This review systematically examines the paper's strengths and limitations, situates it against at least ten competing models and theories in decision theory, statistical treatment rules, cascade deferral, metareasoning, and decision-focused learning, and articulates the ontological and epistemological verticals underlying the evolution of its central themes. Possible extensions and ideation pathways are proposed. All references follow Harvard style. KSCCN review article, 11 October 2026. Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun, ORCID 0000-0001-6845-2853. items.title: Delegation Is Not Assistance: Agentic AI and Assessment Governance in Higher Education - A Comparative Documentary Analysis of 12 Universities
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) assessment policies in higher education have centred on originality, disclosure, and permission to use AI. Agentic AI, which can plan, use tools, access platforms, and act with limited human intervention, challenges this logic because it can take over the whole action chain of an assessed task rather than only generate content. This study examines how assessment governance changes from GenAI to agentic AI. Using exploratory comparative documentary analysis, public central guidance from 12 universities was theoretically sampled: six agentic-aware cases and six GenAI-dominant comparators, with a retrieval cut-off of 3 October 2026. Documents were coded on six dimensions using a directed framework informed by Bacchi’s “What’s the Problem Represented to Be?” approach. All agentic-aware cases distinguished agentic AI from GenAI, and most set explicit delegation and access boundaries, whereas no comparator explicitly addressed agents operating institutional systems on a student’s behalf. The comparators, however, were strong on evidence of learning and task-level transparency, and programme-level assurance was sparse in both groups. The study proposes the Delegation-Evidence-Access (DEA) framework, which moves governance from tool permission towards responsibility allocation, and derives four assessment contexts and a task-, course-, and programme-level implementation model. Implications for Malaysian higher education are discussed. Findings are descriptive, based on selected public documents, and not representative; no inter-rater reliability was assessed.

items.title: Effects of AI-Supported Learning on Independent Cognitive Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Instructional Scaffolding and Learner Characteristics
items.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis will examine the effects of AI-supported learning on objectively assessed cognitive performance when AI assistance is unavailable during assessment. It will cover intelligent tutoring systems, traditional chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI across educational stages and subject areas. Technology characteristics and instructional support functions will be coded separately, allowing overlapping features rather than imposing mutually exclusive technology categories. The primary objective is to estimate the effects of AI-supported learning compared with non-AI learning conditions on independent cognitive performance. Secondary objectives are to examine direct comparisons between AI-supported instructional approaches and whether effects vary with baseline learner characteristics and instructional support functions. Relevant support functions include hints, explanations, feedback, worked examples, self-explanation prompts, verification and revision prompts, adaptive learning pathways, and restrictions or fading of AI assistance. Randomized and non-randomized controlled intervention studies will be synthesized separately. A distinct observational evidence stream will examine associations between actual AI use, such as usage frequency, help-seeking, and verification behaviors, and eligible cognitive outcomes. These associations will not be combined with intervention effects or interpreted as causal evidence that a particular use behavior improves learning. Eligible outcomes include objective measures of knowledge and understanding, application and transfer, other cognitive skills, and composite achievement, which will be analyzed separately. The first eligible post-intervention assessment and subsequent delayed assessments will be distinguished. Assessments must be completed without AI; access to non-AI resources will be recorded separately. Unclear AI permissions will remain awaiting clarification rather than being treated as confirmed eligibility or grounds for automatic exclusion. Two human reviewers will independently screen records, extract key study information, and assess risk of bias, with disagreements reconciled. Analyses will account for overlapping reports, shared samples, dependent effect sizes, and differences in study design and comparison conditions. Moderator analyses will depend on sufficient comparable evidence. Within-study learner moderation will be distinguished from between-study associations. The review aims to clarify whether benefits of AI-supported learning persist when learners are assessed without AI, and which learner characteristics and instructional support functions may be associated with those benefits. No uniformly positive effect or ranking of technologies is assumed. Before registration, preliminary scoping and pilot screening examined 30 purposively selected candidate reports, and selected results from four reports underwent trial extraction to assess feasibility and refine the protocol. This prior exposure to study findings is disclosed. A comprehensive systematic database search, formal independent duplicate screening, complete data extraction, and quantitative synthesis have not yet been conducted. Substantive subsequent changes will be documented through dated amendments.

items.title: Exploring artificial intelligence usage preferences among medical students in Iran: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical education, offering opportunities to enhance learning, research, and clinical preparation. Although previous studies have explored medical students’ attitudes and acceptance of AI, evidence regarding their AI usage preferences remains limited, particularly in developing countries where AI integration into medical education is still evolving. Understanding these preferences is essential for designing context-appropriate educational strategies and responsible AI integration. This study aimed to examine the preferences and patterns of AI usage among students at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences (SUMS), Iran. This descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted in 2025 among undergraduate and postgraduate students at SUMS. Using stratified random sampling, 384 students were recruited. Data were collected between July and October 2025 using a validated self-administered questionnaire (AI-UPSS; Cronbach’s α = 0.935), assessing AI usage across eight domains. Responses were rated on a 4-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using one-sample t-tests, independent t-tests, and one-way ANOVA in SPSS version 24, with a cutoff mean score of 2.5. The highest mean preference scores were observed in Research & Writing (Mean = 2.66 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Self-learning/Education (Mean = 2.61 ± 0.81, p = 0.010). Moderate preferences were found for Curiosity & Entertainment (Mean = 2.36 ± 0.81, p = 0.001) and Health Counseling (Mean = 2.40 ± 0.96, p = 0.044). The lowest scores were reported in Design & Programming (Mean = 1.54 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Art (Mean = 1.68 ± 0.77, p < 0.001). Significant gender differences were observed in Art ( p = 0.010), Self-learning ( p = 0.027), and Health Counseling ( p < 0.001). GPA was significantly associated with Content Development ( p = 0.004), Design & Programming ( p = 0.031), and Art ( p = 0.032), with higher usage among students with lower GPAs. Undergraduate students showed significantly higher preferences across several domains, including curiosity and health counseling ( p < 0.01). Medical students primarily use AI for academic, research, and self-directed learning purposes, while engagement with technical and creative applications remains limited. AI usage preferences are influenced by academic level, gender, and GPA rather than age or field of study. These findings underscore the need for structured, level-specific AI education to promote effective and ethical AI integration in medical curricula.
